title: Nebulae: the clouds where stars are born
intro_sentence: A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust between the stars. Some glow red, some shine blue, some are black silhouettes, and the cold, dark ones are where new stars begin to form.
body_paragraphs: An emission nebula makes its own light. The hottest and most massive young stars, of spectral type O, flood the gas around them with ultraviolet light, which strips the electrons from hydrogen atoms. When protons and electrons recombine, they give off light at specific wavelengths. The strongest in the visible range is hydrogen-alpha, a deep red, so these glowing clouds, called H II regions (ionised hydrogen), look red or pink in photographs. NASA compares the effect to a neon sign. Other elements add their own colours: oxygen, sulfur, nitrogen. Because the glow needs ultraviolet light from O stars, which live only a few million years, an emission nebula is a sign that massive stars have formed there recently.

A reflection nebula does not glow on its own. Its stars are too cool to ionise the gas, so the cloud only scatters their light, and dust grains scatter blue light more strongly than red, which gives these nebulae a blue cast. A dark nebula is dust dense enough to block visible light from everything behind it, so it appears as a silhouette against brighter stars or glowing gas. Dark nebulae are the visible face of molecular clouds, cold clouds in which hydrogen is bound into molecules. The largest hold between about ten thousand and ten million solar masses and span roughly 15 to 600 light-years. The same kind of cloud can look like any of the three, depending on whether a hot star, a cooler star or no star lies near it.

Stars form inside molecular clouds, some as cold as about 10 kelvin. Gravity gathers the denser parts into clumps, and the clumps into dense cores. A core that collapses heats at its centre and becomes a protostar; the contraction continues until the centre is hot enough to fuse hydrogen. The whole process can take a million years or more. Only a small fraction of a cloud's mass, about 2 per cent, ends up in stars. One cloud breaks into many cores at once, so stars are born in groups: the Trapezium cluster in the Orion Nebula, with its four bright stars at the core, or the several thousand stars of the cluster NGC 6530 in the Lagoon Nebula.

The Orion Nebula (M42), about 1,410 light-years away, is the closest large star-forming region; its Trapezium stars carve a cavity with their ultraviolet light. The Eagle Nebula (M16), about 5,540 light-years away, holds the Pillars of Creation, columns 4 to 5 light-years tall that young stars just outside the frame are eroding. The Lagoon Nebula (M8), about 4,150 light-years away, has funnels each about half a light-year long. The Tarantula Nebula (30 Doradus), in the Large Magellanic Cloud about 160,000 light-years away, is the most active star-forming region in the Local Group of galaxies.
